text: Right now, there are more homes for sale in the McAllen metro than at any point in thirty-six years.
In October, about thirty-four hundred homes were listed. In the fall of twenty twenty-one, there were fewer than a thousand.
And this fall, mortgage rates jumped back above seven percent. In early October they hit seven point four, the highest since twenty twenty-three.
So is this a buyer's market you should jump on, or a warning sign for anyone building or lending in the Valley? Let's look at the numbers. This is RGV News.
Start with supply. Housing economists use months of inventory: how long it would take to sell every listed home at today's pace.
Six months is balanced. Below six favors sellers. Above six favors buyers.
In May twenty twenty-one, the McAllen metro had about two months of inventory. Homes got multiple offers. Buyers waived inspections.
Builders answered that shortage. Hundreds of new subdivisions went up across Hidalgo County.
Now the McAllen metro sits at about nine months of inventory. That's firmly a buyer's market.
One private lender who finances builders put it bluntly. Some new subdivisions in Weslaco, he said, are "ghost towns, completely empty."
You might expect prices to crash. They haven't. They're slipping.

The median listing price in the McAllen metro peaked at two hundred eighty thousand dollars in October twenty twenty-three. This October, it was two hundred fifty-five thousand. That's about nine percent lower.
The median sale price has barely moved. It's held near two hundred forty-five thousand since twenty twenty-three.
Homes are also sitting longer. In October, the typical McAllen listing stayed on the market about seventy-eight days. In the fall of twenty twenty-one, it was forty-eight.
What's changing is the discounting. In October, about one in six McAllen listings had a price cut.
Builders are adding rate buy-downs, appliance packages, and warranties. In some cases, new homes are priced below resale homes.
One example: a new three-bedroom on Gumwood Avenue in McAllen listed at two hundred seventy-five thousand in February. By August, the asking price was down to two fifty-nine.
Earlier this year, buyers caught a break. In late February, the thirty-year fixed rate dipped to five point nine eight percent.
McAllen sales jumped. In January, closings were up twenty-one percent from a year earlier.
Then inflation came back. Energy prices climbed with the conflict involving Iran, and rates followed. By October, they were back above seven percent.

Here's what that means in dollars. Take a two-hundred-fifty-five-thousand-dollar home with ten percent down. At the February rate, principal and interest is about thirteen hundred seventy a month. At today's rate, it's about fifteen hundred seventy.
That's about two hundred dollars more every month, before taxes and insurance.
And sales cooled. In September, McAllen metro sales were down eight percent from a year earlier.
The deeper problem is income. Over the past decade, median home prices rose seventy-five percent in the McAllen metro. Median household income rose sixty-three percent.
In Brownsville-Harlingen, prices more than doubled. Incomes rose sixty-seven percent.

The median household in Hidalgo County earns about fifty-six thousand dollars a year. Spend thirty percent on housing, and that's about fourteen hundred a month. At today's rates, principal and interest alone on a median-priced home is more than that.
Then add property taxes and insurance. One Brownsville broker says deals fall apart when buyers see a monthly note near twenty-eight hundred dollars.
Taxes are also pushing more homes onto the market. One Valley realtor says owners now tell her they can't keep paying the property taxes on their salary, so they're selling.

Realtors say the real demand is between one hundred fifty and two hundred fifty thousand dollars. But with lots now costing fifty to seventy thousand, builders say a two-hundred-thousand-dollar house is nearly impossible.
And the Valley isn't one market. Brownsville-Harlingen has far fewer listings, about fifteen hundred, and roughly six point seven months of inventory. That's close to balanced.
Prices there are higher, though. The median Brownsville-Harlingen listing was two hundred ninety-seven thousand dollars in October, down from a peak of three twenty-one in twenty twenty-two.
But Brownsville sales fell seventeen percent through August, back to twenty-nineteen levels, even with SpaceX and LNG hiring nearby.
So what should you do before twenty twenty-seven?
If you're buying, this is leverage. Nine months of inventory means you can ask for price cuts, closing costs, and rate buy-downs.
If you're building, the gap is the product. Townhomes, smaller homes, and build-to-rent can reach the one-fifty to two-fifty range that resale can't.

If you're lending, watch carry costs. Banks are tightening construction loans. Some builders now pay private lenders around thirteen percent, versus about eight at a bank. A home that sits for nine months gets expensive.
Our watch list: weekly mortgage rates, monthly inventory in McAllen, and whether Brownsville sales recover as port and SpaceX payrolls grow.
The Valley isn't crashing. It's resetting. The deals go to whoever does the math first. This is RGV News.
